paper.title_en: Investigating the Impact of SAX J1808.4-3658's Very Bright Thermonuclear X-ray Burst on the Accretion Disc with NICER
paper.abstract_en: We analyse a bright thermonuclear X-ray burst from the accreting millisecond X-ray pulsar (AMXP) SAX J1808.4-3658, the brightest burst detected by \textit{NICER} to date, to explore interactions between thermonuclear burst radiation and the accretion disc. This burst features a remarkable soft (<1.5 keV) excess in its spectra. For the first time, we simultaneously detect a reflection signal and the signature of an evolving persistent component, with our fits producing a peak persistent scaling factor $f_{a,1} = 59.6\pm0.6$. We find a high peak reflection fraction ($f_{r,1} = 0.82\pm0.15$) and a peak bolometric burst blackbody flux below Eddington (0.68$L_{\mathrm{Edd}}$) despite signatures of photospheric radius expansion. We detect a raised $N_\mathrm{H}$ ($\approx$34% above persistent emission) and raised disc blackbody temperature ($\approx$15% above persistent emission) during the burst's tail. This is the first time that spectroscopic evidence consistent with burst-induced disc heating has been found. We interpret that disc heating could cause the disc to puff up and inhibit burst photons, explaining the high reflection fraction and below-Eddington burst luminosity during the burst peak. We find an increasing count rate starting from $\approx$150s before the burst onset. Spectral analysis revealed a thermal component that evolves towards hotter temperatures closer to the onset of the burst. This is the second detection of this phenomenon from an AMXP. Lastly, we find that both the double-peaked structure and the "pause" in the rise are energy-dependent.
